rationale: B wins because it turns the facts into sharper founder choices, especially the line: "It is the only angle you can pitch this week without first answering the accuracy question." A is smart, but "Deel is giving away the compliance layer it used to sell" reaches past the supplied facts and then asks proof to clean up the mess. The difference is discipline: B knows which story can move now and which one will eat the spokesperson alive without audit data.
gaps_in_A: "Deel is giving away the compliance layer it used to sell" is not grounded tightly enough; the update says the AI tool is included for existing customers, not that a previously sold compliance layer is now free.
"The prevailing belief in the category is that AI can now absorb compliance work" invents a market consensus the update does not provide. The missing accuracy data is enough; do not decorate it.
"compresses the ground under standalone compliance vendors" needs competitor and pricing evidence. A admits that later, but the headline-level claim gets ahead of the proof.
"Who eats the fine when the AI misclassifies a contractor?" overlaps with the accuracy-disclosure angle. A needed a lower-rung customer or buyer workflow angle instead of two accountability cousins.
gaps_in_B: "at no extra charge rather than selling a new SKU" goes beyond "included for existing customers." Permanent pricing, renewals, and new-customer treatment still need confirmation.
"legal instrument" is hotter than the fact pattern. The tool flags risks; B should not imply it makes legal determinations unless Deel says customers rely on it that way.
"One employer, one bad contractor call" is the right shape but not yet a story. Without a named customer and a real flag, it is a placeholder with good posture.
